---
title: "Summarizing a posterior distribution"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false
  message: false
---

The [posterior-distribution page](posterior-distributions.qmd#updating-a-continuous-parameter) defined the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model. We now summarize its $\operatorname{Beta}(43,79)$ posterior without changing the estimand or the sampling caveat.

A posterior expectation uses the probability-weighted averaging operation from the [expected-value page](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd), and posterior variance uses the [expected squared-deviation definition](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd). Conditioning has the reference-set meaning developed on the [conditional-probability page](../foundations/conditional-probability.qmd), while the Bernoulli update assumes conditionally [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd) cells given their shared parameter. The credible intervals below condition on the observed data; the earlier [confidence-interval page](confidence-intervals.qmd) instead varied random endpoints over repeated samples.

We will distinguish center from spread, construct interval and directional summaries, transform each posterior value before summarizing a nonlinear quantity, and then match each reported number to the claim it can support.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-posterior-summaries
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
resource_share <- K / N
unit_count <- 1L
alpha_post <- unit_count + k
beta_post <- unit_count + n - k

posterior_mean <- alpha_post / (alpha_post + beta_post)
posterior_variance <- alpha_post * beta_post /
  ((alpha_post + beta_post)^2 * (alpha_post + beta_post + 1))
interval_probs <- seq(.025, .975, length.out = 3L)
posterior_quantiles <- qbeta(interval_probs, alpha_post, beta_post)
probability_above_resource <- 1 - pbeta(
  resource_share, alpha_post, beta_post
)

stopifnot(N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, k == 42L)
data.frame(
  mean = posterior_mean,
  variance = posterior_variance,
  q025 = posterior_quantiles[1],
  median = posterior_quantiles[2],
  q975 = posterior_quantiles[3],
  probability_above_known_resource_share = probability_above_resource
)
```

## Center and spread

For $\Theta\mid\mathbf z\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha',\beta')$,

$$
\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=\frac{\alpha'}{\alpha'+\beta'},
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]
=
\frac{\alpha'\beta'}
{(\alpha'+\beta')^2(\alpha'+\beta'+1)}.
$$

The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior mean is `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_mean)`, and its variance is `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_variance)`. The posterior median is `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_quantiles[2])`. The mean minimizes posterior expected squared-error loss; a median minimizes posterior expected absolute-error loss. Thus neither center is automatically the preferred estimate without a loss function.

## Credible intervals and directional probabilities

An equal-tailed 95% credible interval uses the posterior quantiles

$$
\left[
F^{-1}_{\Theta\mid\mathbf z}(.025),
F^{-1}_{\Theta\mid\mathbf z}(.975)
\right].
$$

For the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model it is [`r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_quantiles[1])`, `r sprintf("%.6f", posterior_quantiles[3])`]. Holding the observed sample fixed, the exchangeable model and prior assign 95% of posterior mass to this interval. A confidence procedure instead repeatedly generates samples while holding the parameter fixed and calibrates how often its random endpoints cover that parameter.

An equal-tailed interval places $2.5\%$ of posterior mass below its lower endpoint and $2.5\%$ above its upper endpoint. A highest-posterior-density interval instead seeks a shortest high-density region and need not allocate equal tail mass. For a skewed posterior the two summaries can differ; neither is automatically appropriate without a reporting purpose.

The probability that the counterfactual exchangeable share exceeds the known resource share is

$$
\mathbb{P}\!\left(\Theta>\frac{K}{N}\mid\mathbf z\right)
=
\int_{K/N}^1
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

Its value is `r sprintf("%.6f", probability_above_resource)`. This comparison does not make $K/N$ uncertain and should not be read as evidence that the file's known proportion has changed.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-posterior-summary
#| fig-cap: "Exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation posterior density. The shaded region is the central 95% interval; the vertical line is the known share in the complete UniMorph table."
plot_grid <- data.frame(theta = seq(0.15, 0.58, length.out = 1000L))
plot_grid$density <- dbeta(plot_grid$theta, alpha_post, beta_post)
plot_grid$inside <- with(
  plot_grid,
  theta >= posterior_quantiles[1] & theta <= posterior_quantiles[3]
)

plot_opacity <- 0.18
ggplot(plot_grid, aes(theta, density)) +
  geom_area(data = subset(plot_grid, inside), fill = "#8B1A1A", alpha = plot_opacity) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = resource_share, color = "grey30", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Modeled share of t-initial lexeme cells", y = "Posterior density") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Transform before summarizing

Suppose the linguistic report uses odds rather than a probability. Define

$$
G(\Theta)=\frac{\Theta}{1-\Theta}.
$$

The mean of the transformed quantity generally differs from the transformation of the mean:

$$
\mathbb{E}[G(\Theta)\mid\mathbf z]
\ne
G\!\left(\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z]\right).
$$

For a beta posterior, the first expectation exists when $\beta'>1$ and equals $\alpha'/(\beta'-1)$.

```{r}
#| label: transform-unimorph-posterior
expected_odds <- alpha_post / (beta_post - 1)
odds_at_expected_probability <- posterior_mean / (1 - posterior_mean)
odds_interval <- posterior_quantiles[c(1, 3)] /
  (1 - posterior_quantiles[c(1, 3)])

data.frame(
  expected_odds = expected_odds,
  odds_at_posterior_mean = odds_at_expected_probability,
  odds_q025 = odds_interval[1],
  odds_q975 = odds_interval[2]
)
```

Compute the estimand within each posterior value or draw, then summarize that distribution. The same rule preserves joint uncertainty when a contrast depends on several parameters.

Here `expected_odds` is $\mathbb{E}[G(\Theta)\mid\mathbf z]$, while `odds_at_expected_probability` is $G(\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z])$. Their displayed difference is the numerical consequence of transforming after rather than before averaging. Likewise, `qbeta()` maps posterior probability levels to interval endpoints and `pbeta()` integrates the normalized density below a threshold.

## Matching the summary to the claim

A center answers a location question, an interval describes posterior concentration, and a directional probability answers a threshold question. None of these summaries turns the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model into a model of Turkish token frequency. The row remains a lexeme--paradigm cell, and the independent-draw assumption remains a modeling assumption imposed for instruction.

## Recap and forward link

1. A posterior mean and median correspond to different loss functions.
2. Equal-tailed and highest-density intervals summarize concentration differently.
3. A directional probability integrates posterior mass relative to a fixed threshold.
4. Nonlinear estimands must be transformed before their posterior distribution is summarized.

The [conjugate-prior page](conjugate-priors.qmd#collecting-powers) next derives the algebra that produced this posterior family.

## Check your understanding

1. Which loss functions select the posterior mean and median?
2. How does a 95% credible interval differ from a 95% confidence interval?
3. Why does $\mathbb{P}(\Theta>K/N\mid\mathbf z)$ not update $K/N$?
4. Why should a nonlinear estimand be transformed before it is summarized?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Squared-error loss selects the posterior mean; absolute-error loss selects a posterior median. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. A 95% credible interval contains 95% posterior mass conditional on the model, prior, and data; a 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its reference model. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. $K/N$ is computed from the complete UniMorph table and remains fixed; the posterior probability concerns the counterfactual superpopulation parameter $\Theta$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. For nonlinear $G$, $\mathbb{E}[G(\Theta)\mid\mathbf z]$ generally differs from $G(\mathbb{E}[\Theta\mid\mathbf z])$, so the transformation must be applied to each posterior value first. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
